objective_for_doctor: Evaluate a 55-year-old man presenting with foot pain and cramping during exercise, and diagnose the underlying condition.

turns.content: Hello, I'm your doctor today. What brings you in today?

“Doctor, for the past six weeks I’ve had a tingling pain in the sole of my right foot that shows up when I raise my foot above chest level during exercise. Also, when I use the incline on the treadmill, my right calf cramps and I have to stop a few times, but the pain goes away after a few minutes of rest.”

Do you have any low back pain, buttock pain, or pain/numbness shooting down the leg when this happens?
Do you have any low back pain, buttock pain, or pain/numbness shooting down the leg when this happens?

“Doctor, I don’t really have low back or buttock pain, and I don’t feel shooting pain down the leg—it's mainly the tingling in the sole of my right foot that starts with certain exercise positions, and the calf cramps with the incline.”
Does the right calf cramping happen predictably after a certain amount of walking or incline and then reliably improve within a few minutes of stopping?

“Doctor, yes—it happens pretty predictably after a certain point on the incline, and stopping brings the cramps down within a few minutes every time. The tingling in the sole also tends to show up when my foot is raised above chest level during exercise.”
Have you noticed your right foot being colder, paler, or having weaker pulses than the left, or any color change with elevation?
“Doctor, I haven’t noticed my right foot getting colder or paler than the left, and I don’t recall any color changes with elevation, but I’m not sure about the pulse differences between sides.”
Do you have any vascular risk factors such as smoking, diabetes, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, or known artery disease?
“Doctor, I have type 2 diabetes and I’ve been smoking two packs a day for 34 years, but I don’t know about any known artery disease or my cholesterol or blood pressure levels.”
Is the tingling/pain in the sole brought on specifically by ankle position—like pointing the toes up or down—or by tight shoes, and do you ever get numbness or burning at rest or at night?

“Doctor, it seems more tied to the ankle position—when I raise my foot above chest level during exercise the tingling comes on, and I don’t notice much of it with just tight shoes. I don’t typically get numbness or burning at rest or at night; it mainly shows up with those exercise positions.”
Have you had any recent leg injury, new exercise routine, swelling, or one-sided calf enlargement?

“Doctor, I haven’t had any leg injury or swelling, and I haven’t noticed any one-sided calf enlargement. I did start exercising regularly about two months ago, and that’s when the calf cramping with incline and the tingling in the sole during higher foot positions began.”
How old are you, and are you male or female?

[DDX] Peripheral arterial disease causing intermittent claudication, Popliteal artery entrapment syndrome, Chronic exertional compartment syndrome, Tibial nerve entrapment/tarsal tunnel syndrome, Lumbar spinal stenosis/radiculopathy

Most likely is vascular claudication from peripheral arterial disease: predictable calf pain with incline/exertion that resolves within minutes of rest, plus major risk factors of diabetes and heavy smoking. The sole tingling with leg elevation/exercise could reflect ischemia provoked by position/exertion.

Popliteal artery entrapment is also worth considering because symptoms are exercise-related and can be position-dependent, though it is less typical at age 55 and with your strong atherosclerotic risk profile.

Chronic exertional compartment syndrome can cause exertional calf pain that stops with rest, but the vascular risk factors and position-related foot symptoms make it less likely.

Tibial nerve entrapment/tarsal tunnel could explain plantar tingling, especially if ankle position provokes it, but it would not as well explain classic exertional calf cramping relieved by rest.

Lumbar stenosis/radiculopathy is less likely given no back/buttock pain or radiating symptoms and the very reproducible exertional pattern.

This needs in-person evaluation because PAD can be limb-threatening over time and is also a marker of cardiovascular risk. Key next steps would be pulse exam and ankle-brachial index, ideally with exercise ABI if resting
